Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the best of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Victory! (Jaya).
May the sage Vyāsa purify you, he who is ever-present for our happiness,
and whose pure Sarasvatī flows through the three paths and is full of sweetness.
Questioned again by Śaunaka at Naimiṣa, the son of Lomaharṣaṇa related the wondrous account of the birth of the enemy of Kaiṭabha upon the earth.
Having heard the story of the Bharatas, Janamejaya was filled with joy;
he then respectfully questioned Vaiśampāyana concerning the lineage of Viṣṇu.
Being thus questioned by King Pṛthu, he, having bowed down with devotion to the Lord Hari, the cause of the worlds, related the story.
In the beginning, the imperishable Lord Viṣṇu emitted the waters;
he cast his seed into those called "men" (nara), by which he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
Then that golden egg came into being, from which Prajāpati was born;
he created Manu and the other principal ones, as well as the Prajāpatis beginning with Kardama.
And Dakṣa, whose lineage consists of his grandsons, assigned separate kingdoms to all living beings, beginning with those named Soma and the rest.
Once, a son of Aṅga, the Prajāpati of the Atri lineage, was born of Sunīthā, the daughter of Mṛtyu; he brought about the destruction of stability.
There was a king named Svarva, whose mind was turbid with sin; due to his aversion toward the prescribed duties, he was like a calamity incarnate for his subjects.
When he remained unsubdued despite being entreated many times,
the sages then seized that exceedingly powerful one and cast him down.
Agitated by the fire of their wrath, they churned his left thigh;
from that, there emerged a dark man, Svarva, overwhelmed with fear.
Addressed by Atri with the words "Sit down," he became the progenitor of the Niṣādas;
thereafter, the sages churned the right hand of Vena.
Then, from that lotus-hand with its copper-colored leaf-like fingers,
there emerged the illustrious Pṛthu, whose eyes were wide like those of the Grandfather Brahmā.
The Jāgava bow of that king, who showered gold,
shone like the blazing mass of flames of a radiant fire.
When Vena had gone to heaven through his grace, Pṛthu, the son of Vena, became the first among kings; he came and was himself worshipped with jewels by those who were like mines of gems.
His movement was unimpeded both on water and on rock;
and bards, panegyrists, and heralds, newly arisen, praised him.
Commanded by that powerful one for the sake of providing sustenance for living beings, she fled in the form of a cow;
he, armed with a bow, pursued her.
Having fled with speed through all the worlds up to the world of Brahmā,
she finally beheld him with his weapon raised, her face turned back toward him.
Seeing no means of protection, she spoke to him with palms joined in reverence:
"O protector of the earth, abandon your anger; protect me, a woman."

"This undertaking of mine toward you is for the sake of the livelihood of my subjects;
the harming of one is praised for the purpose of protecting many lives."
"Having expanded myself, I shall sustain all creatures;
if you do not grant sustenance to the worlds, then become my daughter."
Thus commanded by the king, the earth, bowing down, replied:
"Being your daughter, I shall provide for the livelihood of your subjects."
O Lord, level the regions that are formidable with heaps of rocks;
let this happen for everyone, O Māyā, so that you may pour forth milk.
Having heard this, Pṛthu of vast fame split apart the massive mountain peaks with the tip of his bow, whereby the earth became clearly defined.
Then, making Svāyambhuva Manu the calf and using the hollow of his cupped hands as the vessel, he milked the earth— which bore his own name— as its yield of crops.
It is heard that in ancient times the sages milked the earth for asceticism and the Veda;
Soma was the calf, Bṛhaspati the milker, and the vessel was gold.
And the ancestors milked this earth, which is like nectar, using a silver vessel; they took Yama as the calf and Antaka as the milker. (Bhājana-vinaya 19.29)
The Nāgas milked poison into an alābu gourd vessel, making Dhṛtarāṣṭra the milker and Takṣaka the calf; it was a bestower of strength. (Bhājana 19.30)
The earth was milked for magical power by the Asuras in an iron vessel;
at that time, Prahlāda was the calf and Madhu, the son of Danu, was the milker.
In former times, the Yakṣas also milked [the earth], making Dhaneśvara their calf;
they obtained a terrifying milk that grants invisibility when placed in an unbaked clay vessel.
Blood was milked by the Rākṣasas;
auspicious fragrances were milked into lotus bowls by the Gandharvas and Kinnaras, with Sumālin acting as the calf.
Taking Mount Meru as the milker and the mountains as the vessel,
they milked the multitude of jewels and medicinal herbs, making the Himalaya the calf.
Then, from the trees, milk was drawn into a vessel made of *pālāśa* leaves;
thereafter, the *sāla* tree assumed the role of the milker, and the *plakṣa* tree that of the calf.
"Because of the teaching of the victorious first king Pṛthu that 'the earth belongs to everyone at all times,' this deed of his is truly marvelous."
***** The Milking of the Earth ***** Having heard this account of Vainya’s deeds, Janamejaya was struck with wonder;
he questioned the sage regarding the narrative of the Manvantaras, and the sage spoke as follows. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4.19.37)
In the beginning, Svāyambhuva Manu existed, and at that time there were the seven ṛṣis,
Marīci, Atri, Pulastya, and the others...
the gods known as the Tuṣitas.
The third Manu was named Auttama; at that time, the seven ṛṣis were the sons of Vasiṣṭha, and the Ṛbhūs were the inhabitants of heaven.
The fourth Manu was Tāmasa, during whose interval the seven ṛṣis were Pṛthu,
Gārgya, and others, and the gods who dwell in the three heavens were the members of his assembly.
Raivata was also the fifth Manu; at that time, the seven ṛṣis were headed by Vedabāhu, and the gods were the Abhūtarajasas.
Then the sixth Manu was Cākṣuṣa; during his interval, there were seven sages headed by Bhṛgu, as well as the gods known as the Lekhas.
Now that these six sons of many offspring have passed away,
the glorious seventh Manu, Vaivasvata, reigns today.
Kaśyapa, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Bhāradvāja, Gautama,
Kauśika, and Jamadagni— these seven today are the great ṛṣis.
The deities were Aśvin, Rudra, the Maruts, the Vasus, and the Ādityas;
and the sons of this Manu were kings headed by Ikṣvāku.
Now, Sāvarṇi will be the future Manu; during his interval, the seven ṛṣis are Rāma, Vyāsa, Kṛpa, Ātreya, Drauṇi, Gālava, and Kāśyapa.
There will be four future Manus, the Merusāvarṇas;
for each of them, there will be nine other [groups], and they will each have their own respective seven ṛṣis in succession.
The sixth Manu is named Roca, and the seventh Manu is called Bhautya;
these are the fourteen Manus from whom the Manvantaras proceed in succession.
Seventy-one complete sets of four yugas, plus a little more—
this is the limit established by calculation for each individual Manvantara.
Then, when those fourteen Manvantaras have passed,
at the end of the Kalpa, the entire world dissolves within Viṣṇu.
And it arises again; thus it revolves like a wheel.
This course of existence, characterized by the destruction of eons, is without beginning or end.
Now, regarding this present Vaivasvata interval of Manu Sāṃprati,
let the origin of his lineage be heard in connection with the Harivaṃśa.

***** Description of the Manvantaras // 2 // ***** The Sun, Vivasvat, a treasury of great splendors, was born from Kaśyapa; he possessed a formidable form, a mass of intensely blazing and fierce radiance. (Bhājana-kalpa 19.54)
"By good fortune, this one within the egg has not died due to his own increased radiance;
because he was thus addressed by his father out of affection, he became renowned as Mārtaṇḍa. (Bhājana-vinaya 19.55)
His name was Saṃjñā, and his beloved was Lāvaṇyanalinī,
the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ Prajāpati, the creator of many wonders.
In her, the Sun begot a son, Manu Śrāddhadeva, as well as a daughter, Yamunā; because they were twins, they were given these names.

Then Saṃjñā, though possessed of fortitude and steadfastness, could not endure that distorted form of the sun of sharp rays and terrible splendor; she was like a night-lotus [overwhelmed] by the light.
Having assumed her own reflection— which was identical in form and produced through the application of *māyā*—
she went secretly into the presence of her father-in-law.
Dismissed by that proud man with the words, "Go to your husband," the Vaḍavā,
feeling ashamed, departed for the Northern Kurus.
Then, from the wife of the Sun who was of the same caste as Saṃjñā, a son named Sāvarṇi was born; he was the next Manu, begotten upon Chāyā while the Sun’s conduct remained unknown.
And Śanaiścara was the second; out of affection, Chāyā showed them greater love than she did toward her other two sons.
The eldest Manu, being patient, endured that; but Yama did not forgive it. Long ago, by chance, his mother was struck by him as a child out of childishness.
Enraged, she cursed him, saying, "May your feet fall off!
Hearing this, the radiant one became apprehensive and prepared to curse her back in anger.
Having gone quickly to the house of Tvaṣṭṛ, he related the account of Saṃjñā:
"This exceedingly fierce radiance of yours, though it be true, Saṃjñā cannot endure."
"A mare is roaming secretly there in the forest, grazing on the young grass"—
having learned this from the speech of Tvaṣṭṛ, he was led into that very delusion.
Eager to behold his beloved, Tvaṣṭṛ, unable to restrain his own splendor,
fashioned the Sudarśana discus with that very brilliance.
Then the sun, the beloved of the lotus, who possesses a lovely form, became the companion of the enemy of Kaiṭabha in the destruction of the darkness of the Daityas.
Having gone to the forest, he beheld his beloved in the form of a mare;
there she was being trampled by him in the form of a horse as she struggled.
She turned her face away out of fear of contact with another;
then, by means of a nasal exhalation, she [received] the seed of Vivasvat.
From that [seed] he emitted the two Aśvins, the Nāsatyas, who were born as twins;
then, having recognized the gentle god Saumya as the Sun (Divākara), she [conceived].
Nijarūpavatī followed him and went to her home;
Manu became the Prajāpati, and Yama became the lord of the ancestors.
The two Aśvins shall be the physicians of the thirty gods, the Yamunā shall be a river,
and there will be another Prajāpati, Manu, the son of Savarṇā.
Among the planets, Śanaiścara was the seventh and moved slowly;
Ikṣvāku, Śibi, Śaryāti, Nābhāga, and others were the sons of Manu.
When they had been born, Manu, desiring sons, performed a sacrifice to Mitra and Varuṇa;
from that, a daughter of playful splendor was born to him.
Named Iḍā, her face like a lotus, she followed the command of that mantra; she bowed down, illuminating the sky with the radiance of her shimmering jewel-ornaments.
Thinking, "I am a portion of Mitra and Varuṇa; this is their dwelling," she departed.
She, who was worthy of virtuous conduct, was welcomed by the two of them as their daughter.
She obtained that boon: "You shall become the son of Manu.
Then, having turned back, she departed, moving with the gait of an elephant.
Having seen her, who possessed eyes like those of a young deer, Budha, the son of the Moon,
obtained Purūravas as his son through union with her.
Having cast off her female form, she became the king named Pradyumna;
his sons were Utkala, Vinatāśva, and Gaya.
Ikṣvāku’s son was Tṛṇabindu, and his son was Kakutstha.
In that lineage appeared Kuvalāśva, who, by the word of Uttaṅka, [became a horse].
He slew the terrible great asura named Dhundhu, who was hidden within the sands,
by whose breaths the earth was scorched.
In the lineage of King Kuvalāśva, Āruṇi was born from you;
because of his abduction of the daughter of a Paura, he became known by the name Satyavrata.
Cursed as a son of the lowest caste, he lived in a desolate place;
meanwhile, during that twelve-year period of hardship, there was no rain.
On the shore of the ocean, Viśvāmitra abandoned his wife along with their son;
she, having tied her middle son by the neck, was prepared to sell him.
Restrained out of compassion by Satyavrata, who provided him with a livelihood,
that son of Viśvāmitra, Gālava, became one whose throat was bound.
When the family priest Vasiṣṭha said, "Why do you not give her up to me as your father?",
the prince Satyavrata became filled with indignation.
Then, deluded by the curse, he killed the wish-fulfilling cow as she was grazing and made it food for himself and the sons of Gādhi.
Due to his father's anger, the killing of the cow, and the eating of food that had not been consecrated,
Vasiṣṭha cast a triple curse upon him out of fear of [the king's] retaliation.
Having bestowed upon his father, who was named Triśaṅku, the status of a Brahmin, Viśvāmitra became his officiating priest, by whom he ascended to heaven in his physical body.
His son was Hariścandra, who shone resplendent during the Rājasūya sacrifice;
in his lineage was King Sagara, by whose sons the ocean (sāgara) was made.
Born together with poison from his stepmother’s gift,
he conquered the frontier regions of his father, who had previously wronged him.
He established the Kāmbojas— who were devoid of Vedic study and the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, marked with physical stigmata,
and shaven-headed— into the role of guardians of the lower regions.
He fashioned the Śaśakas with heads topped by skulls, those with disheveled hair, the Pāradas, the Pahlavas, the Yavanas, and others, who were characterized by their beards.
In his lineage was Dilīpa, whose son was Bhagīratha;
it was through him that the river Bhāgīrathī attained the status of a daughter upon the earth.
In his lineage there was a king named Rāma, the son of Daśaratha;
and from his son Kuśa, many royal sages were born.
This is the lineage of Ikṣvāku; as for his brother who was about to die, the Śakas became his sons. Nābhāga’s son was born.
Ambarīṣa was the protector of the earth, and the sons of Vṛṣṇi were the Vṛṣṇis;
the sons of Śibi were those bold in battle, and the sons of Śaryāti were born.
Sukanyā was married by Cyavana, and their son was Antabhūpati;
Raveṇī was his daughter, and in former times he lived together with her.
He went to the world of Brahmā to hear the Gāndharva in the presence of Brahmā;
then, after many yugas had passed like a mere fraction of a moment, [he returned].
Having returned to his own city, he beheld Dvārakā surrounded by the Vṛṣṇis;
it remained untouched by the power of Time, as if it were still dwelling in the realm of Brahmā.
He gave the young Revatī to Balabhadra,
and having given away his daughter, he departed for the cave of Mount Meru to practice asceticism.
The sixth son of Ikṣvāku was named Riṣṭa, and his two sons were Vaiśyas who,
through the power of asceticism and yoga, became stainless and attained the status of Brāhmaṇas.
The seventh was Karūṣa; his sons were the Kāruṣa kings.
And the eighth was Pṛthuka, who became a Śūdra due to the killing of his guru’s cow.
These eight sons of Manu were the brothers of Ikṣvāku;
thus these were the upholders of the lineage of Śrāddhadeva Manu upon the earth.

***** The Lineage of Manu // 3 // ***** Having been questioned by the king in the course of a discussion on ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), the sage spoke of the ritual for the ancestors (*pitṛkalpa*); and at the conclusion of his reply, Bhīṣma addressed Yudhiṣṭhira. (Bhājana 19.106)
When the ancestors are honored in the śrāddha rite with three funeral cakes (piṇḍas) representing three generations,
they nourish living beings as deities even within various states of existence.
When the funeral cake (piṇḍa) was offered by me for my father, Śantanu, at the time of the śrāddha ceremony,
a hand— delicate as a lotus and adorned with a noble bracelet— rose up.
Having observed that, I offered the funeral ball (piṇḍa) upon the kuśa grass itself; because it followed the ritual prescribed by the scriptures, it brought him satisfaction. (Bhājana 19.109)
"Therefore, having obtained the boon of dying at my own will— the most excellent of boons—
he instructed me at that time regarding Mārkaṇḍeya, who had arrived."
I questioned the deity regarding the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*) and the fruit for those who sacrifice to the ancestors;
he, being questioned by me while I was practicing austerities on the peak of Mount Meru, spoke thus.
In the presence of Sanatkumāra, the Blessed One, that treasury of splendors,
spoke thus to Brahmā in the past, having seen those gods who were performers of self-sacrifice.
"How is it that these do not sacrifice to me?"—with this curse he deluded them;
they all, their consciousness lost, propitiated the Lotus-born One.
At his command, they asked their own sons about the expiation;
then, purified by those expiations and through the instruction in ritual action and knowledge, they were cleansed.
Because of their weightiness, they were told by their own sons, "Go, dear sons";
yet these fathers are to be honored, even though they are the children of the gods.
The gods declare that for those who lack ancestral offerings (śrāddha), all ritual acts are fruitless;
in sacrifices devoid of such offerings, the Rākṣasas consume the fruit.
Therefore, the ancestors are mutually [related] to the gods, and the hosts of ancestors as well;
through the śrāddha, Soma is nourished, and he in turn sustains all living beings.
Through the *śrāddha* rite, the ancestors are pleased and nourish the fathers and grandfathers of men everywhere, even those who have entered the wombs of animals.
Four of their groups possess form, while three groups are formless;
they are the nectar-eaters who enjoy yoga, renowned as the Vairājas.
Their daughter was named Menā, the beloved of Himavat;
their son was the illustrious Maināka, the father of the great mountain Krauñca.
Menā had three daughters who practiced difficult austerities;
the eldest among them was named Aparṇā, who became Bhavānī, the beloved of Bhava.
The one who was called Umā was restrained by her father through asceticism;
she became the second wife of the sage Devala, known as Ekaparṇā.
Jaigīṣavya’s third wife was Ekapāṭalā,
who was the mind-born daughter of the Marīciputras, the Pitṛs.
The excellent river named Acchodā, flowing from the eastern Acchoda Lake,
beheld her father with longing, not recognizing him.
Falling by his curse, yet with a limit established by his grace,
she was born from the womb of a fish in the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age.
Gandhakālī bore Vyāsa as her son from Parāśara;
the sons of Pulastya are the Pitṛs known as the Barhiṣads, who dwell in heaven.
Their mental daughter, a yoginī named Pīvarī,
will give birth to offspring through whom Śuka, the son of Vyāsa, shall be born.
Having made the mother the daughter of King Brahmadatta,
these three classes of ancestors are formless and have renounced all karma.
Those who, being honored, contemplate the Soma-devas and the Mānavas are the Pitṛs known as the Mūrtas; others, the Somapas, are consumers of nectar.
Their daughter was Gaurī Mānasī, whom the Brāhmaṇas worship;
others, however, are the sons of Aṅgiras, the Pitṛs who are devoid of faith.
Those Kṣatriyas were performers of sacrifices, and among them was a maiden named Yaśodā;
she was the mother of King Dilīpa, who performed a thousand sacrifices.
The Ājyapa Pitṛs are the sons of Prajāpati Kaśyapa;
Vaiśyas always worship them, as does their mental daughter.
The mother of Yayāti, the lord of the earth, was named Virajā;
the sons of the sage Vasiṣṭha were the Pitṛs known as Sukālās.
Those [deities] are to be worshipped by the Śūdras alone; their daughter is the river Narmadā, who was beloved by Kurukutsa, and whose son was King Trasaddasyu.
These four classes of ancestors are embodied deities of the [four] castes,
for whom Manu, the god of funeral rites (Śrāddhadeva), ordained worship in age after age.
In a Śrāddha ceremony, the weapon of those who consume the *svadhā* offering— whether it be made of silver or marked with silver—
should be worshipped preceded by offerings to Soma and Agni.
These ancestors are to be worshipped when they are free from anger and full of grace;
for them, devotion—which is like a wish-fulfilling creeper—is of great fruit.
"You shall see all this at the sacrifice— how the Brahmins, having fallen away from the worship of their ancestors due to their neglect of dharma, will regain their own station."
"Understand the nature of faith for yourself," having said this,
Sanatkumāra gave me divine vision and vanished.
Then, in the course of time, I saw those seven brahmins in Kurukṣetra:
Vāgduṣṭa, Krodhana, Hiṃsra, Piśuna, Svasṛma, and Kavi. (Bhājana 19.140)
And they were named Pitṛvatī because they followed their father’s example;
furthermore, they were formerly the heirs of Gārgya Kauśika, their preceptor.
Having set out on the road, the fools, afflicted by hunger, prepared to kill a cow;
even when they were being restrained by the poet and their own brother-in-law.
Then, his anger unabated, he who was devoted to his father said to them:
"In every way, this is an improper act of yours, censured by all living beings."
"If this undertaking is difficult to accomplish, let it be performed preceded by a *śrāddha* ceremony.
Having heard this, they all carried out the rite as he had instructed.
Then, having been cursed at that time because of their violence,
they were born as hunters in the Daśārṇa country, established in their own work and devoted to truth and virtuous conduct.
Due to the fruit of the *śrāddha* performed in another birth, their memory was not lost;
they were free from enmity, tranquil, patient, devoid of anger, and possessed the wisdom of the Creator.
And those hunters, who were devoted to their mothers and intent on serving their father, cast away their bows and water-vessels for their parents and became lifeless. (Bhājana 19.147)
Then, on Mount Kālāñjana, in a bower of thickets of blossoming creepers,
those deer who remembered their former births became agitated by fear and exhaustion.
Unmukha, Nityacakita, Stabdhavarṇa, Sulocana,
Ghasmara, Piṇḍita, and Nādī— these are the names corresponding to their respective movements.
Those celibate practitioners, patient and having cast off their former learning,
went to the slopes of Mount Meru and there relinquished their lives.
Today I see the rows of trees rising from the slopes of the Kālāñjana mountains, which flow toward Meru, visible upon their golden peaks.
Then, on an island in a pure river, where the sands were strewn with waves,
those young *cakravāka* birds became celibate students (*brahmacārin*).
Free from possessiveness, free from longing, patient, without enmity, without accepting gifts,
tranquil, and composed— such are the yogins, those who fly through the air.
And there those swans were born, devoted to asceticism and yoga,
in that place garlanded with lotuses and water-lilies blooming and stirred by the gentle breeze.
While sporting in the water, they beheld the king named Vibhrāja,
whose lotus-like faces surpassed a lake in beauty.
Seeing him, who had arrived by chance at the edge of the grove of creepers on the riverbank to drink,
the younger bird looked upon him as if he were the lord of Śacī.

The heroes, Virocana and the others, stood facing the battle;

Reassured by Viṣṇu, the gods rushed forward;

Displaying thousands of rainbows with the rays of his vajra,
Yama— dark-complexioned, riding upon a buffalo, and wearing a great necklace of stars— appeared.
Śvetāśva, marked with a garland of jewels and possessing the radiance of the sun, stood like a dark mountain with hanging clouds and waterfalls, appearing like Varuṇa himself.
In his chariot he shone upon Kailāsa like a towering peak of jewels;
Hemārka was in a golden chariot, wearing golden armlets.
The giver of wealth (Kubera) took away from Mount Meru its splendor, which was enjoyed by the sun’s heat;

The son of Śārṅga, whose banner is Garuḍa and who wields the blazing discus and mace,

Then Hari, adorned with the Kaustubha gem, shone as he ascended [the mountain], appearing like a single mass of light formed by twelve suns joined together at the horizon.

As the battle proceeded, [the arrows] rose up like heaps of golden iron shafts,

"This most great illusion of the Daitya is exceedingly difficult to resist."

the quarters of the sky were illuminated by showers of flowers, as if by the fame of Hari.
While the guards were stupefied by sleep,
Vasudeva, his intention prompted by them, himself secretly performed the exchange of the two fetuses.
Having placed his son in the house of Nandagopa and taking that [Nanda’s] daughter, he,
filled with apprehension and fear, abandoned her in the bedchamber of Devakī’s womb.
Then, having awakened and exclaiming in wonder, "A daughter has been born!",
the guards showed her to Kaṃsa while she was still wet from the waters of the womb.
Then, at their command, she was struck upon that broad stone surface;
with many arms bearing blazing weapons, she entered her own [body] like a flame of fire.
Adorned with necklaces and star-garlands, her face as beautiful as the moon,
she was like the night personified, generating bewilderment in all beings.
She shone with two earrings radiant with the luster of precious swan-jewels,
like the sky when the orbs of the moon and the sun are fixed at the points of sunrise and sunset.
Adorned with peacock-feather ornaments and decorated with a peacock-banner,
she was dark-complexioned like the rainy season when it possesses Indra’s bow and swelling clouds.
With their hair-locks adorned by crowns with three peaks that laugh loudly with various jewels,
they appeared like the earth graced by the Rohiṇa mountain.
Accompanied by hosts of spirits, laughing and repeatedly making a loud noise,
she tore through the darkness and, threatening Kaṃsa, addressed him.
O Kaṃsa, at the time of your destruction, when you are being dragged away by your enemy,
I shall tear open the life-force within your body and drink your blood.
Having spoken thus, Kātyāyanī departed for her desired destination from heaven;
and the son of Ugrasena trembled, ashamed at his fruitless endeavor.
Having gone there, he prostrated with his head at Devakī’s feet and, having appeased her, spoke thus:
"O Mother, those fetuses have been destroyed by Time."

***** The Birth of Kṛṣṇa // 11 // ***** Fearing [the king], Vasudeva abandoned the son of Rohiṇī, whose splendor was as beautiful as the cool-rayed moon, right there in the house of the cowherd Nanda. (Bhājana-vrata 19.519)
Having entrusted the elder infant Saṃkarṣaṇa to Yaśodā,
and while the news of Kṛṣṇa remained hidden, he became absorbed in anxious thought for him.
Urged by him who desired the welfare of his son, Nandagopa abandoned the formidable Vṛndāvana, which was infested with serpents and the thorns of demons.
At the edge of the Govardhana forest, where the trees along the Yamunā were lush,
he established Vraja, surrounded by many herds of cattle, free from all obstacles.
In which the cātaka birds were gladdened by the deep, resonant, and rumbling sound [of the clouds],
and the breeze was filled with the fragrance of ghee from the whirlpools of ripening grain.

In that forest where the herds of cattle were hidden by their calves upon reaching it, and where the young deer stood with motionless limbs at the sweet, low-toned singing of the cowherd women; Bhmj_19.524.
On the banks of the Kālindī, amidst the swings of *vānīra* creepers,
the emerald-hued Kṛṣṇa played with his brother, who was as bright as the moon.
That sprout born in the forest grew like the Yamunā flowing into the Ganges;
it lay motionless beneath Śakaṭa’s cart, having been satiated with breast milk while asleep.
Once, having left him behind, Yaśodā went to the Yamunā;
then he, having awakened, slowly began to move his hands and feet repeatedly.
He wept, marked as if by streams of milk from the radiance of his teeth;
with his mouth wide open in a yawn, he stretched his feet upward.
With one foot he overturned the cart, casting it down;
in the meantime, Yaśodā approached, her breasts overflowing with milk.
Seeing the cart broken, she who was devoted to her son trembled;
taking up her infant son, who remained unharmed, she spoke thus as Nanda became filled with apprehension.
"By whom has this cart been broken, other than by the strike of an intoxicated bull?
When asked thus, the children replied, "By Kṛṣṇa. (Bhājana-mañjarī 19.531)
***** The Breaking of the Cart ***** Then,
while the world was asleep during the festival of Kṛṣṇa, a night-stalker named Pūtanā arrived at night, her breasts flowing with milk through her illusory power. Bhmj_19.532 //
Desiring the death of that infant, she placed her breast to his mouth;
but he, having pulled it away, cut it off along with her life-breaths.
When Vyāghraghoṣā had been slain, Nandagopa, together with his wife, rose up in terror and was like one repeatedly sinking and surfacing in the ocean.
Then, having learned the news and filled with wonder and joy,
the couple said nothing at all outside, out of fear of Kaṃsa.
***** The Slaying of Pūtanā ***** Capable of traversing the three worlds, he rained down joy upon his kinsmen with his gentle footsteps and his mild coming and going. Bhmj_19.536.
In the forest, Kṛṣṇa and Saṃkarṣaṇa grew with time,
like two young lions filled with the pride of youth.
With their bodies beautifully adorned, they shone while playing as children,
as if embracing the earth to protect it, being capable of removing its burden.
With eyes like lotus petals and moving, curling locks of hair,
the two lovers made their white pearl necklaces appear as if they were smiles upon their throats.
The bodies of those two became equal in their excellence of beauty and sweetness;
indeed, when great beings take refuge together, there is surely no contradiction between their shared purpose.
While the Lord, the protector of the three worlds, was there tending cows at his own will,
the gods felt a longing for those cowherds who were blessed by his company.
When Yaśodā was unable to hold him, because of his great speed,
the wise woman then bound Dāmodara around the waist with a rope (dāman).
Having quickly dragged away the mortar bound with ropes,
he moved about the forest, playful and free from fatigue.
The cowherds were struck with wonder at his dragging of the mortar—
even though the world was not amazed by him who possesses the steadfastness of Mount Mandara as its support.
Having reached two massive *arjuna* trees growing close together on the bank of the Yamunā,
he stood between them and forcibly pulled at the mortar.
Then, uprooted by the force of his strength, those two trees fell down with such speed that they caused a deep agitation in the waters of the Yamunā.
Seeing that, the cowherd boys, agitated by fear and wonder,
went to Yaśodā and spoke to her with voices faltering from excitement.
"O you of negligent character, deluded while sleeping in comfort, those two trees worthy of worship have fallen upon your son. (Bhājana 19.548)
"Go and see that child, who has been delivered from the great fear of the gods.
Upon hearing this, Yaśodā trembled like a moth in a fire and went forth.
Beholding her son between those two great trees, she experienced,
in succession, terror, joy, and wonder.
Then all the elder cowherds, having approached in great agitation, said:
"By whom have these two divine protectors of the settlement been struck down?"
There was no thunder from clouds, so what talk can there be of lightning in a cloudless sky?
There is no elephant here intoxicated; why then is this sudden destruction of the two trees?
While the circle of cowherds was speaking thus, Nanda took up his son;
releasing him, he looked at Yaśodā with resentment.
When Nanda-gopa had departed with his followers, everyone in every house reproached their own wives; there was even a sense of pride born from the talk of breaking trees.
***** The Felling of the Tree ***** Then Saṃkarṣaṇa and Acyuta, having somewhat outgrown childhood,
wearing blue and yellow garments and marked with side-locks of hair like the wings of a crow, wandered in the forest. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.55.5)
With their flower-ornaments pressed upon their heads, they resembled two young Naga princes who, by the jewels at the tips of their protective forehead-marks, create the illusion of bearing fruit.
Adorned with the sprout-like radiance of peacock-feather ornaments,
they were like two sons of the Pārijāta tree, overflowing with the nectar of loveliness.
With voices as sweet as the natural resonance of short flutes,
they were like two young kiṃnaras seated upon the rocks of a lofty mountain.
With graceful agility in their skillful spinning of the large balls that flew upward,
they were as lovely with their variegated garlands as two sons of the Vidyādharas.
Holding in their hands small bows marked with arrows,
the two heroes, Rāghava and Lakṣmaṇa, appeared as if they had returned once more to the forest.
Dwelling there, those two lotus-eyed ones, magnificent in their pride, shone with the slight, emerging grace of fresh youth.
Keśava, though eager for the delights of a new forest, did not take pleasure there, for the medicinal herbs and trees were sparse and withered from long enjoyment.
Having instilled terror in the cowherd settlement by means of hidden wolves created through his illusory power,
he went to the beautiful banks of the Kālindī at the edge of Vṛndāvana to sport.
Once Gokula had settled there— free from fear and providing a refuge worthy of service— a certain joy arose from the enjoyment of the new forest among the community of cowherds.
Then there appeared a dark-complexioned woman with newly risen breasts, like the fresh rainy season of Kṛṣṇa, having assumed its festive splendor.
In the sky, the new clouds, resembling moving young elephants,
acted like the rising columns of smoke from the fire of love in the hearts of women separated from their lovers.
Then the wind, forcibly generated by the sighs of thoughts from women separated from their lovers, was as if fanning the victorious King Smara with fans.
Upon the earth, the filaments of the *ketaka* flowers shone with the white radiance of lovely smiles,
like the cool-rayed moon’s digits shattered when crushed by a cloud.
Circles of cranes moved through the sky with a deep,
resonant roar, like the massed luster of the tusks of intoxicated lordly clouds-elephants.
Through the rainbows of the clouds and the dancing of peacocks in the forests,
a rivalry, as it were, arose between them, each vying with the other's mass of radiance.
With its thick groves of *tāla* and *kadalī* trees washed by the rains and casting deep shade,
the earth shone like a young woman who has just bathed with oil.
With the arching brows of her galloping horses and laughing with masses of foam,
she wandered through the forest of Yamunā like a youthful woman intoxicated by youth.
A certain splendor of the clouds,
possessing the beauty of a garland of lightning, shone like a mass of molten gold clinging to the peak of Mount Meru.
Terrified by the dark clouds, flocks of royal swans departed for some unknown place;
the beds of night-lotuses went forth as if to search for the moon that had long been lost.
At that time, which was overflowing with the fragrance of kadamba and kuṭaja flowers and filled with joy,
Saṃkarṣaṇa spoke to Kṛṣṇa during that season of those separated from their lovers.
Behold, O Kṛṣṇa, the sky filled with clouds that glide along and laugh with the foam of their cranes, like the waters of the Yamunā.
The dark body of the clouds, which wear lightning as yellow garments and hang with garlands of forest flowers,
shines like your own dark form.
Having heard these words of his elder brother, which were an ornament of affection, Hari,
whose own ornaments are his playful graces, rejoiced in the Madhurābharaṇa forest.
***** Description of the Monsoon ***** Then,
once, when the entire world seemed as if newly born through the clearing of the rains,
Kṛṣṇa was wandering in the forest without his brother. (Bhājana-mālā 19.579)
Surrounded by cowherd boys whose outstretched arms were like massive trunks, he reached a vast banyan tree that seemed to have risen up as if to measure the very sky.
It rose up as if out of curiosity to behold the peaks of the Kulādris, which are inhabited by Vidyādharas and frequented by the gods of the Tridaśa realm.
We pay homage to the tree named Bhāṇḍīra, the noble and beautiful shade that fulfills all hopes, the ornament of the earth, and the palace of the vine-like women.
Seeing that affectionate kinsman of bliss, Śauri moved incessantly at his side,
joyful and providing entertainment with song and instrumental music.
Then he beheld the Kālindī, whose spray was like the ichor from the temples of the elephant of the world, with its undulating waves curved like the long braid of hair of the Earth.

She, possessing the excellent luster of the *tāpiccha* flower, was like a night that had turned into liquid, adorned with a garland of stars consisting of foam-bubbles, as is fitting for a meritorious person.
It was marked by the swelling hoods flashing with the leaping of wide-gaping fish,
appearing like an army of serpents curved by the expanse of its waves.
Her face was like a blooming lotus, her eyes were like blossoming blue water-lilies;
the fullness of her breasts was like that of ruddy geese, she was dark-complexioned, and her smile was as white as a swan.
With its mountain caves filled with gems melting from the heat of the fierce sun,
it was as if a stream of emerald liquid had begun to flow, surging with whirlpools.
In some places she was motionless as if asleep, in others agitated as if intoxicated;
in some places she was as if in a swoon from the force of poison, and in others as if bitten by a serpent.
In one place she was like one frightened and hidden; in another, like one agitated and distressed; in another, trembling with intense agitation; and in another, like one possessed by pride.
Seeing that river, which had the high water-jars of the tall breasts of the intoxicated cowherd women as its lofty waters,
Kṛṣṇa rejoiced at it as if it were a captivating young woman.
Then he beheld [the ocean], deep and terrifying as the bottom of the netherworld (pātāla),
agitated by hundreds of waves curved like the fierce, frowning brows of Time (kāla).
Stained by darkness, exceedingly fierce, and causing fear without cause—
[they avoid] that Lord from afar, just as everyone avoids a wicked man.
Even now, with its heart burning with the thought, "The world has not yet been swallowed by me," it seems to sigh incessantly through the waters that act like rising columns of smoke.
It was filled with terrible, venomous serpents dwelling in its banks and hollows,
like a lake devoid of moon, sun, and stars that brings terror to oneself.
Having gazed for a moment at that [lake] which was difficult to agitate even from afar, Hari thought:
"In this [lake] dwells that serpent named Kāliya, who is fierce with the Kālakūṭa poison."
He whose appearance was dark as a cloud and who struck terror into all living beings,
by him this bank of the Yamunā was defiled with poisonous breaths.
Thus, this one, intoxicated by excessive pride, deserves destruction here;
for generally, such a manifestation of mine leads to the ruin of the evil-minded.
Having reflected thus, he climbed onto a young *kadamba* tree at the edge of the lake;
having girded his loins, he leapt from the sky down into the water.
By the roaring black cloud that descended with great force,
the water was agitated and rose up with its crest of terrifying waves.
Arising from the crashing of waves resembling mountains leaping from afar,
there occurred a terrible clashing sound that struck the very heavens.
Then Kāliya appeared, terrifying with his emission of fire and his poisonous flames, five-faced and red-eyed.
Enveloped on all sides by his ever-increasing wealth, which was like a mountain of collyrium, the water submerged the sky.
Within the circle of flames blazing from his anger, it was quickly dissolved,
creating the illusion of a second submarine fire in the waters.
The successive flames of poison born from the crushing of his teeth suddenly reduced the rows of trees on the riverbank to ashes.
Then Kṛṣṇa, being encircled by the black serpent Kṛṣṇa,
shone like a tamāla tree entwined by the dark waters of the Yamunā.
Seeing Govinda surrounded on all sides by the lord of serpents and his followers, whose fangs emitted poisonous flames, the cowherd boys [were terrified].
Terrified and dropping their balls, they ran to Vraja and cried out:
"This Dāmodara has fallen into the terrible waters of the Kālīya!"
Surrounded by a serpent as formidable as Time itself and emitting fierce venom,
they all— headed by Nandagopa— departed for the lake upon hearing these words.
While Nanda the cowherd stood motionless with his gaze fixed upon the face of his son, which was enveloped by the serpent, his heart trembled with doubt at the sight of the fresh lightning-flash.
While the women were crying out with piercing lamentations, tormented by Yaśodā’s harsh words as if they had been struck by the poison of passion, and were thus exceedingly distressed; Bhmj_19.611.
Having reached the shore with Saṃkarṣaṇa, he was awakened by a mere sign;
he struck the body of a serpent, whose expansive form was terrifying, with his two arms.
Having stepped upon him with his two feet, Hari emerged from his bonds;
then Madhusūdana, bending down the circle of hoods blazing intensely with jewels, ascended the broad central head.
Then he, the teacher of all the worlds, both moving and stationary,
began to trample with his footsteps as if dancing with graceful movement.
Then, his pride shattered and his fortitude failing, with the fierce poison vomited forth,
he addressed Kṛṣṇa in words that fell from his mouth as he choked with blood.
Terrified, I am to be protected by you with all your soul;
this gesture of joined palms, this wretchedness, is my very merit for life.
Having heard this, Dāmodara said to the lord of serpents:
"O you of inauspicious conduct, let this lake be frequented by you alone."
Therefore, go to the ocean if you desire to live;
there my footprints shall serve as your protection against Tārkṣya.
Thus, when the serpent had departed with its followers at his command,
the cowherds, filled with joy and wonder, went along praising Kṛṣṇa.

***** The Subduer of Kāliya // 16 // ***** Then Haladhara and Acyuta entered the forest, dark with its vast *tāla*, *hintāla*, and *tamāla* trees, which resounded with the playful quarrels of birds. Bhājana-mālā 19.620.
Their minds intoxicated with the joy of tasting the fruit of the five *tāla* trees,
the two of them wandered there, intent on the grand display of childhood play.
Then a Daitya named Dhenuka arrived, who dwelt in a grove of palm trees;
he was a fierce donkey-like creature with formidable manes and a broad, imposing chest.
Surrounded on all sides by his large-bodied followers riding donkeys,
there arose a dense thicket of palm trees that seemed filled with rising smoke.
Then Dhenuka, his eyes blood-red with intense rage,
tore up the earth with his hooves, desiring to slay Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
As if issuing a summons to the Daityas dwelling in the netherworld,
and as if striking them with his neighing, he whose weapon was his teeth as fierce as thunderbolts [neighed].
With his tail wildly whirling, he rushed impetuously toward Saṃkarṣaṇa,
like a turbulent cloud with a single crest blown by the wind rushing toward the moon.
Then, biting his teeth without agitation, he turned his face toward the west, with his back turned to Rauhineya for the sake of striking him.
Taking up that striker with his two hooves,
he hurled him to the top of a palmyra tree, just as Halāyudha might cast down a fruit seeking its harvest.
With his thighs, hips, and shoulders broken, and his hard bones shattering,
he fell to the ground along with the palm fruits, all his efforts rendered futile.
Then, when he had been slain along with his followers, and Khara’s prowess destroyed,
that vast palm grove became free from obstacles and fit for habitation.

***** The Slaying of Dhenuka // 17 // ***** Having gone once more to the Bhāṇḍīra forest, those two, delighting in play, sported with the sons of the cowherds through various games of leaping and wrestling. Bhmj_19.631 //
Then there arrived a Dānava named Pralamba, adorned with ornaments of wild flowers as ear-ornaments, his true form concealed under the guise of a cowherd's dress.
Capturing their hearts through his play, he repeatedly delighted them;
at one time, having mounted his shoulder, he carried away the elder brother of Keśava.
Having abducted her, he of swift motion revealed his own form,
by which the quarters of the sky became as if covered by a veil of darkness out of sheer fear.
Upon his head, which resembled the peak of the mountain of collyrium,
shone a crest-jewel, tawny like a mass of flames from a forest fire.
The column of smoke and fire issuing from his mouth shone like a blue and yellow banner hanging from the archway of his fangs.
Upon the shoulder of the Dānava, which was as formidable as the peak of a dark blue mountain, the son of Rohiṇī bore the splendor of an autumnal cloud.
Being swiftly carried away by him, he assumed a human state;
he was made to remember his ancient form, which was once equal to Keśava.
That which is the supreme abode, the Lord of Speech with faces on all sides,
consisting of all the gods, the Truth, infinite, unborn, and immutable.
Relying on his own vast strength capable of supporting the earth,
the slayer of Dhenuka struck Pralamba on the head with his fist.
From the falling of his fist, the skull of the Daitya’s forehead shattered and split open;
his head, streaked with gushing blood, entered his own body.
When Rāma had slipped from his shoulders, Pralamba’s massive body fell, its two arms hanging down like a mountain.

***** The Slaying of Pralamba // 18 // When Pralamba had been struck down by the powerful Baladeva, and the four months of the rainy season had gradually passed away, [the Lord] proceeded there. Bhmj_19.643 //
As the festival of the sacrifice drew near— a source of intense joy filled with fresh eagerness— the forest-dwellers commenced their preparations.
Then [she appeared], garlanded with the fragrance of *saptacchada* trees, with swans for her anklets,
a face like the pure moon, and eyes like blooming blue lotuses.
Like a young woman invited to that great festival of Vraja,
the autumn season appeared, her garment of sky smiling with the white clouds as its decorative patterns.
There, having learned through the words of Gopa that Kṛṣṇa was performing the sacrifice for the Lord of the Maruts,
he spoke with smiles and white glances, as if emitting the Pāñcajanya conch.
"Ah! How truly ridiculous is this mind of yours;
this sacrifice for Śakra is not fitting, for these cowherds are but deities of the mountain. (Bhājana 19.648)
Thus, at their word, the cowherds proceeded with a mountain-sacrifice;
edible mountains were prepared, from which flowed abundant streams of ghee and milk.
At that sacrifice on Mount Govardhana, where vast quantities of food were gathered,
the earth became as if covered with snow because of the milk-rice mixed with curds.
Adorned with peacock-feather ornaments and crests of flower-garlands,
the cowherds and the cows shone beautifully decorated at that sacrifice.
Upon the mountain peak, the Soul of the Universe, Kṛṣṇa, with a body of supreme mountain-like stature, enjoyed all that which had been offered by them.
Then Kṛṣṇa himself, along with the cowherds, bowed down before that great, divine, and natural body of his own, which was radiant as a mountain and graced by a smile of supreme joy.
***** The Mountain Sacrifice ***** When that great festival had concluded, Indra, blazing with wrath,
commanded the terrible Saṃvartaka clouds to destroy Vraja. (BhP 10.35.42)
Driven by him, those clouds, as dense as the rocks of Mount Nīla, swiftly covered the world like hundreds of nights of the end of time.
With clouds possessing the hue of crushed collyrium and thundering with fierce force,
the ten directions were suddenly swallowed as if by arrogant beings and became invisible.
Then, torrents resembling the trunks of elephants, with the agitation of pillars [of smoke], fell upon the mountain; they were indeed a supreme abandonment of steadfastness.
The black clouds, with their terrifying, loud laughter and falling torrents of water,
shone like waterfalls cascading from dark mountains.
Thus there arose a deluge of water, fashioned from masses of clouds of terrifying expanse, tossing with surging, massive waves.
The earth, submerged in water, fled somewhere as if out of fear of the roaring cloud-demons whose hair was tawny with lightning.
Empowered by Śakra, those terrible beings, marked by blazing thunderbolts,
wrought a slaughter among the cattle with a downpour of falling lightning.
As they cast their eyes upon the eyelids and fell here and there,
overcome by terror and cold, their destruction became terrible.
"This is that commencement of universal dissolution, terrifying with the Puṣkarāvarta clouds;
it has arrived"—thus was the state of mind of the cowherds who were struck with fear.
Seeing that terrible slaughter of the cows approaching toward their destruction,
Govinda, the protector of the worlds, reflected for a moment upon how to provide protection.
Having forcibly uprooted this king of mountains, Govardhana,
I shall make it a vast umbrella and a shelter for the cows standing nearby.
Having reflected thus, the wise one fixed his gaze upon the mountain with his mind,
as if it were a row of blooming lotuses, to endure the moment of its uprooting.
Then, immediately, the Soul of the Universe, accompanied by a great force,
uprooted the mountain with his two arms, its base and summit splitting asunder.
Like serpents that had quickly emerged from Pātāla following the uprooting of a mountain, those [roots] clinging to the base took on the appearance of a network of sinews.
The quarters of the sky shone, draped in silken garments of hoary waves, as waterfalls were formed by the pressure of crushed rocks.
Covered by heaps of yellow orpiment dust, whirled about by the eddies of the wind and cast down upon him, Kṛṣṇa shone as if he were clad in yellow garments.
As he leaped up for a moment, the clouds shaken at his sides created the illusion of wings for the mountains moving through their own courses.
When that mountain had become a parasol for Govinda’s staff-like arms,
the trailing garlands of blossoming flowers created the illusion of a decorative wreath.
"O Vajradhara, today after a very long time these mountains and we ourselves have become free-moving; abandon this pride of having clipped the wings of the earth-dwellers."
Thus, as the Vidyādhara gazelle-eyed women leaped up in terror,
that mountain seemed to speak to them through the sounds of their girdles and anklets.
With the roars of lions that agitated his mane as they surged forward and stumbled,
he seemed to threaten the formidable masses of thick clouds.
He shone in the sky like clouds fallen from the peaks of mountain crests by the leaders of elephant herds, who were agitated by the exertion of uprooting him.
With the pollen from the clusters of flowers on the swaying great trees,
he repeatedly created, as it were, protective circles for the cows.
With its wave-like pearl necklaces shaken by the Siddhas who fell down in terror,
the mountain standing in the sky seemed to laugh at the mountains situated below.
Seeing him, the sky-dwellers said: "Is this a mountain that has arisen?
Unless it be the onset of the dissolution of the world, or an untimely catastrophe."
Then, at the word of Kṛṣṇa, the cowherds, together with all their cattle, entered a vast cave beneath a mountain for the sake of peace.
On that very vast mountain slope, which was windless and devoid of water,
the cows and the cowherds remained, exhausted by their journey and their dwelling.
Then, after seven nights had passed while he was traveling shrouded by rain, the Lord of the Maruts departed together with the clouds, ashamed that his efforts had been rendered fruitless.
Then the Teacher of the World effortlessly settled that heavy mountain, with its vast extent and lofty peaks, back upon its own place.
***** The Lifting of Govardhana // 20 // ***** While that mountain had been held up for seven nights by the one whose emblem is Garuḍa,
the thousand-eyed Indra himself, filled with great wonder, came to see him. Bhmj_19.684 //
Descending from the celestial elephant as if from the mobile Mount Kailāsa,
he beheld Madhusūdana seated upon a rock at Govardhana.
The heat was shielded by the wings of the invisible Tārkṣya,
and the sky was filled with a splendor that seemed almost unreal.
Having a luster like the neck of a peacock and the radiance of molten gold,
it was like a peak of the Indranīla mountain heated by the morning sun.
Beholding Hari, the beloved of Kamalā, wearing the guise of a cowherd,
he praised himself as having a thousand eyes within his mind.
With the masses of rays from the jewels in his crown, earrings, and armlets,
he seemed to be repeatedly casting thousands of rainbows into every direction.
Approaching Keśava, Śakra spoke words befitting his affection,
as if filling the ten directions with the nectar-like luster of his teeth.
O Kṛṣṇa, what is so wonderful about this deed of yours, which surpasses even fate,
for you whose power is so slight yet who are the refuge of the entire world?
The wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenu) exist as supreme beings above all the worlds;
by the command of Brahmā, I am the master of those who are honored even by the gods.
"O Govinda, I have come to consecrate you in the kingdom desired by the cows.
Having said this, he poured water from a jewel-filled jar upon his head.
Having consecrated Upendra and propitiated him again and again, Indra said:
"He who is the son of Janaka—your friend, kinsman, and sister's son—must be protected by you."
O Kṛṣṇa, slayer of Daityas, once Keśin and Kaṃsa have been slain by you,
Dhanañjaya, with you as his ally, will conquer the earth.
Having heard these words of affection from the Lord of Śacī, Kṛṣṇa,
knowing the history of the Bharatas, agreed, saying, "So be it."

Aniruddha too, having obtained that beloved who was difficult to find on earth,
considered himself a worthy vessel for the sovereign wealth of the kingdom of Love.
While he who was born of Pradyumna was sporting with her in secret there,
he was recognized by the guards of the maidens' inner apartments through many physical characteristics.
Commanded by Bāṇa, the son of Bali, out of rage at the insult to his daughter,
the terrible Kiṃkaras set out to slay the son of Pradyumna.
Seeing them— with mouths formidable with fangs, fierce with knit brows, and terrifying— wielding drawn, dreadful swords and bows, the hero Aniruddha [stood firm].
Rising up with an impetuous prowess for the commencement of battle,
he sprang toward the door-bar and rushed forward like a lion toward deer.

The body of that treasury of valor, who was gazed upon by the side-long glances of beautiful women and who embodied the form of the God of Love, shone with the intensity of both heroism and erotic passion.
Taking up the shower of weapons released by them as if it were a garland of flowers upon his chest, he who possessed a voice like the roar of a thundercloud struck down the Dānava warriors.
Struck by those blows, their terrifying bodies shattered,
the survivors who remained fled in fear to where Bāṇa, fierce in battle, was located.
"Who is this that has arrived— a witness to the destruction of Indra’s city— who brings about such agitation, generating both anger and delusion, as is fit for the faint-hearted?"
Let honor be paid to valor, which is like the springtime for the flower of fame;
for this terror born of pride is like an unbearable thunderbolt falling upon a mountain.
At the command of Vīra and Bāṇa,
they rushed back toward Aniruddha with a very great army, accompanied by shouts of defiance.
Clad in golden armor and brandishing various blazing weapons,
they appeared like moving mountain lords at night, illuminated by forests of glowing medicinal herbs.
The son of the son of the Discus-Wielder fought in battle with those who were enraged,
while gazing upon his beloved, whose hands were placed upon her trembling breasts.
Having taken up that sword and the radiant shield discarded by him,
the hero moved in circles and cut down his enemies in battle.
With their heads, shoulders, arms, knees, hands, and bellies severed,
they fell like massive clouds scattered by the wind at the end of an eon.
When the army of the Dānavas had fled and their chariots and elephants were broken,
Bāṇa himself appeared, having rallied his ocean-like host.
Yoked to a chariot that crushed the thirty gods, which was driven by Kumbhāṇḍa, possessed a terrifying roar, and was drawn by a thousand radiant horses; Bhmj_19.1260 //
Exalted by the array of radiant weapons brandished by his thousand arms,
he was like a mountain whose peaks are enveloped by fierce serpents with jewels upon their hoods.
With a crown the color of the sun, adorned with a mass of matted locks blazing with jewels,
he seemed to threaten all splendors with his white silk turban that laughed like a loud peal of thunder.
With a fierce radiance from his earrings as blazing as the orb of the sun,
and with a face made terrifying by the knitting of his brows, he struck terror into the three worlds.
Waved by the broad pearl necklaces that were the rays of the moon,
he appeared like a dark mountain from which a great waterfall was gushing forth.
Adorned with a beard and hair having the luster of refined gold,
he appeared at first like a flame produced from the tips of teeth ground together in rage.
Seeing him rushing forward, roaring with a sound like the clouds at the dissolution of the world and crying out, "Stay! Stay!", the son of Pradyumna did not tremble.
Shrouded by dense nets of arrows released from the forest of Bāṇa’s arms,
he became indistinguishable, like the sun obscured by clouds.

The fierce battle between those two, which caused the trembling of the worlds, became the cause for the shaking of the hair on the bodies of Hari and Hiraṇyākṣa as they remembered [their respective lords].
Then Aniruddha, moving with swift agility, severed his succession of arrows and shafts with a sword and cut through the pole of his chariot.
Then the lord of the Dānavas hurled at him a spear wreathed in flames, marked as if with a red cloth, like a female serpent.
Taking that very [spear] which resembled the fangs of Death in his hand,
the Lord of Dharma, whose prowess was wondrous, hurled it at the lord of the Dānavas, O descendant of Daśārha.
Having pierced Bāṇa’s body, it entered the surface of the earth.
Seeing him torn apart by the spear, Kumbhāṇḍa spoke to Bāṇa: (Bhājana-mañjarī 19.1272)
"Resorting to illusion, fight! For he is difficult to conquer if neglected;
for those who employ illusion, victory is obtained without doubt both in gambling and in battle."
Thus, at the word of Kumbhāṇḍa, Bāṇa took up a terrifying, delusive illusion of darkness and suddenly vanished.
Remaining invisible in the sky, he rendered his body paralyzed with arrows of formidable poison that took the form of serpents, though those arrows were invisible even to the highly fortunate.
Surrounded by serpents blazing with the flames from the jewels on their hoods,
he shone with mottled luster, resembling a sandalwood tree.
The lord of the Daityas set his mind upon the slaughter of Aniruddha, who was bound by the serpent-noose and whose mind remained unshaken in its fortitude.
"This person possesses some great power; he should not be executed as long as he remains unknown.
At these words of Kumbhāṇḍa, the son of Bali desisted.
In the meantime, in Dvārakā, within the inner apartments, a cry went up: "Aniruddha has been carried off by someone! such was the sound that resounded.
There, momentarily overwhelmed by confusion and terrified,
the deer-eyed beloveds of Aniruddha lamented, distracted by grief.
Then, within the assembly hall of the enemy of Kaiṭabha, a very great gathering of the Vṛṣṇi heroes took place, summoned by the sounding of kettledrums.
Then, with tearful eyes, they beheld Acyuta, motionless with anxiety, resembling the seven oceans when they are undisturbed by the absence of wind.
While the assembly of Yādavas was mute, overcome by grief, delusion,
and despair, the wise Vipṛthu spoke to Viṣṇu, the conqueror of the enemies of the gods.
O Blessed One, bestower of fearlessness upon the world, what is this new and inconceivable surge of great sorrow that has arisen even within you?
For indeed, those whose minds are as deep and vast as the great ocean do not undergo the fluctuations of joy and sorrow amidst pleasures and pains.
O Lord, if even you, O Acyuta, are thus tormented by the heat of anxiety,
then now the course of fortitude has become supportless and faltering.
Having entrusted the protection of the three worlds to your arm, O slayer of Jambha,
Indra sleeps, blissfully satisfied by the enjoyment of the fullness of Śacī’s breasts.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, Kṛṣṇa— the cloud that extinguishes the swan-like fame of his enemies— uttered words that were deep and slow.
Disdain for others, through its humiliation, takes root in the heart;
it is truly like ignorance to embodied beings who are terrified by anxiety.
Today, the foot of this scion of the Yadu clan, drenched in the mud of the street, has been cast upon the head by someone with an arrogant mind.
Now that Aniruddha has been captured and taken away,
I suspect our prowess has become nothing more than a mere object of derision for other kings.

Since this humiliation and tearing asunder was inflicted by one who is unaware [of our identity], what can we do? Striking the sky with punishments as fierce as anger would be like striking at nothing.
Let spies move everywhere, both outside and inside,
swiftly at the command of Āhuka, for the sake of finding Aniruddha.
When the enemy of Kaṃsa had spoken thus, the celestial sage Nārada appeared there,
a treasure-house of splendor and an expert in the play of strife.
Seeing the Lord of the World motionless with anxiety, he thought:
"Aha! Is not the ocean agitated by the leaping of a mere young fish?"
As he was thus reflecting, Janārdana performed for him worship preceded by water for the feet and a seat; having been honored, he too spoke.
"Alas! What great delusion is this on your part regarding valor, by which you perceive [him] and yet fail to recognize the deeds of Aniruddha! (Bhājana-vastu 19.1297)
A battle-festival, terrifying with the discharge of various weapons and missiles, took place between Aniruddha and the powerful Bāṇa, the son of Bali.
Your grandson Aniruddha, O Kṛṣṇa, has been carried off by the daughter of the lord of the Daityas;
I think that even Smara, afflicted by love, would lose his mind upon seeing her.
The lotus-eyed daughter of Bāṇa, the thousand-armed son of Bali and enemy of the gods, was named Uṣā; she was a lotus pond of loveliness.
Having learned that his daughter’s secret lover was Durjaya, who brought joy to her heart, and seeing that he was invincible in battle, he bound him with circles of serpents.
Therefore, you must go from here to Bāṇa’s Śoṇitapura, situated at the edge of the sky, to fight; for Dānavas cannot be subdued through conciliation.
Mounting Tārkṣya, you must go to that immortal realm which is difficult to traverse,
where the arrow named Bāṇa is the thunderbolt for the hearts of the enemies of the gods.
When the divine sage had departed after speaking thus, the god Madhusūdana also experienced an equal degree of joy, wonder, and anger.
Then the Blessed One, whose banner is Garuḍa, meditated upon Garuḍa;
and being thus meditated upon, he appeared instantly, radiant as the stainless moon.
The glorious one, the soul of the universe, accompanied by Baladeva and followed by the sons of Rukmiṇī, ascended it with the ease of one climbing a palace.
The all-pervading Lord, dark-blue and radiant, adorned with the Kaustubha gem, shone forth,
surpassing the splendor of the sky when the sun has descended to its meridian.
The splendor of that four-armed one consists of his abundant tree-like arms,
which are sprouted by the radiance of the discus and flowered by the rays of the conch Pāñcajanya.
As he proceeded, beautiful in his yellow garment fluttering in the wind,
he made the sky shine with a golden luster by means of the circles of light from the wings of Tārkṣya.
He was attended by those who had come out of curiosity, reflected in all his jeweled ornaments,
with the sprouts of their turbans turned upward toward the edge of the sky.
Garlands of mandārava flowers, dropped from the lotus-like hands of the wives of the excellent vidyādharas, served as the graceful ornaments for his chaplets.
When that hero was captured along with his sister in battle by the powerful Bāṇa in his own city using serpent-nooses, he remained unbound.
Then he sought refuge in Durgā, who enables one to cross over difficult passages;
he praised with divine names her who is the sister of Mahendra and Upendra.

I bow to the Goddess whose face is like the full moon, who is capable of deluding the wicked, and who is the moonlight that dispels the mass of darkness consisting of the sovereignty of the demon Kaṃsa.
She possesses a graceful form that is terrifying with a mass of light from her blazing trident,
like a sandalwood creeper entwined by fierce, writhing serpents.
With her feet placed upon a buffalo, she was dark-complexioned and adorned with necklaces;
like the Yamunā river, which contains the Kālīya lake and smiles with its foam, she appeared radiant.
With the coils of serpents clinging to her arms like dark sword-blades,
she resembled a lotus pond where a swarm of bees was emerging from the interior of a single lotus.
It was frequented by ornaments of peacock feathers, variegated and possessing a deep blue luster,
like the rainy season attended by clouds flashing with rainbows.
With her hair disheveled and her pure movements languid with passion,
she was like a stalk of black aloe-wood grown upon a peak of the Himalayan mountain.
To Sarasvatī, the royal swan dwelling in the minds of the lords of poets,
whose words are wonderful, sweet, and noble, and whose succession of phrases is beautiful.
[She is] the river that flows with the nectar of the bliss of the equal flavor of consciousness, intent upon quenching the heat of the desert of saṃsāra.
She whose majestic onset was profound with the intensity of the fury of battle, and by whom the gods were inspired with fear due to the arrogance of Niśumbha and Śumbha’s roars; Bhmj_19.1322.
She who makes the twilight worship fruitful, who dwells on the Vindhya mountains, the younger sister of Indra,
whose crest is marked by the crescent moon, and who is adorned with a circle of severed heads.
Dark as a forest of blooming blue lotuses, with eyes like blooming blue lotuses, possessing a deep cavity of the navel, and breasts resembling the frontal globes of an elephant; Bhmj_19.1324.
To the blessed Kātyāyanī, Caṇḍā, Cāmuṇḍā who has destroyed her enemies, Śarvāṇī, Śarvarī, and Śarvā, who is served by the Siddhas and Gandharvas; Bhmj_19.1325 //
She is the terrible Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī, who longs to devour the three worlds,
and whose crest is adorned with a garland of skeletons belonging to the lotus-seated Brahmā.
Auspicious, the bestower of auspiciousness, peaceful, the beloved of Śiva, with a hundred faces,
three eyes, a gentle countenance, and the splendor of the intoxication of the enemy of Madana.
She has the vast ocean of nectar with its swelling foam for her silken garment and a girdle of jewels;
she holds the golden mountain in her hand and is tawny with the rays of the citron fruit.
She who has made a rosary from the revolving circle of constellations,
and who holds in her hand the skull-bowl of the universe filled with the nectar-ocean.
She is the mirror of the sky, which is the vast, blossoming radiance of consciousness;
she wears as necklaces, armlets, and bracelets the serpent-kings of the Śeṣa and other lineages.
She smiles with the stars as her pearls and bears the orbs of the moon and sun;
she is radiant with a crown formed by the peaks of the great mountain-king of jewels, which has three summits.
Adorned with a turban as white as the ocean whose waves are the laughing rays of the sun,
it possesses the splendor of a peacock-feather parasol amidst the clouds of the dissolution at the end of an eon, accompanied by Indra’s bow.
I take refuge in the Mother, who is intoxicated by drinking the dense nectar within the heart-lotus—the stalk of whose lotus-navel is coiled at its tip;
she who, like a female bee, is the progenitor of that which is to be known through the power of the ever-arisen primordial sound (*nāda*).
