Having shattered with his lotus-hued hand this terrible, impenetrable cage of serpents that resembles a wall of diamonds, [he entered].
Constantly pursued on all sides by her own vast splendors,
she entered the sky as if drawing away the lifespans of the lords of the Daityas.
In the meantime, the Blessed One, whose banner is Garuḍa and who possesses great speed,
reached Bāṇa’s Śoṇitapura, which was protected by fire.
The slayer of Kāliya became eight-armed with a formidable form,
bearing the conch, discus, mace, lotus, arrow, Śārṅga bow, sword, and shield.
Halāyudha became like the vast snowy mountain with its thousand peaks, possessing a thousand bodies and faces.
And Pradyumna became the Sanatkumāra-kalpa;
while those very forms were vast, the earth trembled.
With the circles of the oceans agitated and solidified by the gusts of wind from Tārkṣya’s wings,
there arose an indescribable tumult at the onset of the dissolution of the worlds.
Then Halāyudha, overcome with wonder, spoke to Kṛṣṇa:
"Why have we suddenly become radiant with the luster of gold?"
The protector of Bāṇa’s city, whose banner bears the emblem of Tārkṣya, said to him:
"Agni, the Āhavanīya fire, stands here before us, uplifted in wrath."
In this world, it appears as if an untimely twilight through his splendor;
now this task shall depend upon Suparṇa.
When Śauri had spoken thus, Tārkṣya, shaking the ocean with the flapping of his wings,
took up the Gaṅgā and brought the fire to a state of calm.
Then other terrible fires, the attendants of Rudra, rose up, filled with masses of flames whose crests appeared like gaping jaws.
In their midst, Aṅgiras, adorned with the blazing flames of his radiant trident,
shone like Mount Sumeru marked by the orb of the sun.
With a crescent-shaped arrow, Hari cut down the fierce trident of his assailant,
just as adverse fate thwarts the desired object of one's efforts.
Struck by Śauri with a great weapon by Sthūlākarṇa, he—
having already felled his enemy— fell down like a fire consumed by fire.
Then, when the army of Bāṇa had been shattered along with its fire-pits and was in a state of agitation,
Janārdana blew his conch Pāñcajanya, which was as pure as his own fame.
By that great sound, which crushed the mass of winds, there arose a resonance as harsh as the clashing of the entire expanse of the worlds.
Then, having entered Bāṇa’s city, he whose banner bears Garuḍa reached that great ocean of Daityas, agitated and prepared for battle.
Hari caused that shoreless army to be covered with arrows sharpened on stone by the fire-weapon,
which were as red as bound crimson execution-cloths.
Then, quickly descending from Garuḍa out of a passion for battle,
the hero whose weapon is the plow fought with the enemies of the gods.
In that abode of the Daityas, which was as dark as a pure tamāla tree,
he shone like Airāvaṇa wandering in a sky filled with dense, blue clouds.
Then, dragged by the plow of Saṃkarṣaṇa,
all the Dānavas fell upon that field of the mace like mountains shattered by the thunderbolt.
Descending from the tip of Suparṇa along with Pradyumna,
Acyuta seized the birds that were the lives of the Daityas with a net of arrows.
Afflicted by the fierce claws and feet of that king of birds and by his flapping wings, they were destroyed; for a moment, they found no peace.
Then, with ashes as his weapon, three faces, three crests, and three feet,
his copper-colored eyes rolling from sleep, he himself became languid with yawning.
With bristling, extremely coarse hairs raised by the cold, resembling a sea-monster (*makara*),
and appearing greyish and withered from exhaustion and delirium, Fever was seen.
Calling out to the son of Rohiṇī, who moves with marvelous skill within the circle of the arena,
he— his body trembling with rage— set his mind upon his destruction.
Resembling the spirit Apasmāra, he hurled that unbearable [weapon] at him,
by which Rāma’s chest was instantly covered with white ash.
The ash arising from that blazing chest fell upon the slopes of Mount Meru;
suddenly flaming, it scorched the mountain peak with a loud crackling sound.
With his entire body glowing from the remaining ashes, his memory obscured and his gait faltering, Tālaketu appeared like one who was utterly intoxicated.
He said, "O Kṛṣṇa, I am burning; I find no composure.
I see the entire world spinning like a potter’s wheel."
Approaching Halāyudha as he was speaking thus, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow embraced him and,
for the sake of pacifying the ashes, seized the fever by his vital energy.
Attacked by him in that terrible battle and blazing with rage,
Jvara hurled from his two fists ashes thick with masses of flaming hair.
For a moment he blazed, yet in that very instant even Kṛṣṇa’s fire was extinguished;
though struck by him with three arms equally, Acyuta did not tremble.
That terrible battle between Kṛṣṇa and Jvara, sounding like a thunderbolt,
became a source of fear for all beings and caused their hair to stand on end.
The luster of golden ornaments appeared upon his tawny body like flames emerging from the pressure of Kṛṣṇa’s staff-like arms.
While he was being pressed firmly with arms by Śauri and cast down upon the ground,
he entered his body unnoticed and swiftly, like the wind.
Possessed by that [demon], the soul of the being became for a moment one who was gasping, yawning, wandering, and sluggish with sleep, stumbling, and experiencing a sudden, wondrous upheaval.
Oh, how extraordinary! The power of things is truly most formidable, since even the Lord of the World underwent a transformation upon contact with the fever.
He created a terrible Vaiṣṇava fever that dispels even the oldest fevers;
by means of that fever, Kṛṣṇa was quickly restored to his former state once more.
Just as Kāliyāri himself, filled with rage, was preparing to slay him,
a voice of terrible sound resounded from the sky.
"O Blessed One, this fever, the attendant of Rudra, must be protected.
Having heard this, Madhusūdana immediately desisted from slaying him.
With palms joined in reverence, Jvara, afflicted by the fever of Viṣṇu, said to him:
"O Lord of the Universe, out of compassion for me, withdraw your own fever."
When his own fever had been withdrawn by Mādhava at those words,
Jvara, preceded by Śarva, bowed to Hari with joy.
To him, who was joyful in heart and saying, "What may I do for you that is pleasing?",
the Enemy of Madhu spoke with words sweet with grace.
"Having prostrated before me, may those men who remember this battle between us— wherein arms are the weapons— and who are devoted to me, be free from all affliction."
Having three feet, wielding a weapon, possessing three heads and tearful eyes—
when meditated upon, he who has your form bestows the bliss of joy upon embodied beings.
May the ancient seers who have neither beginning nor end, the teachers— whether small, middling, or most great—
and Aniruddha, Pradyumna, Bala, and Keśava, destroy all fevers.
Thus addressed with affection by Śauri, Hari-jvara said, "So be it," and with his palms joined in reverence, he spoke while bowing before the tip of the jewel on [Kṛṣṇa’s] crown.
I was created by Hara, the destroyer of Tripura, and by the slayer of Kāliya;
yet I have been conquered by you in battle at the edge of the forest of the Dānavas. What shall I do for you now?
When the fever of Śarva had thus spoken and departed from the field of battle,
Hari, together with his son and his elder brother, mounted Tārkṣya and fought.
Pierced by Kṛṣṇa’s arrows, yet restrained by their devotion to their master,
those proud and excellent Daitya warriors neither stood still nor retreated for even a moment.
Then, their battle arrays shattered, their chariots and elephants broken,
and torn asunder by Dāmodara, the Daityas fled from the battlefield, abandoning it.
Scattered by the Lion like deer, they fled;
like the currents of rivers, they did not return against him.
Having sold your lives—light as the tip of a blade of grass—for a fame as enduring as the end of an eon, where have you gone? For death is everywhere for all embodied beings.
How could they not be struck by fear— by the thunderbolt that shatters the mountain of pride, by the forest fire that consumes the creeper of fame, and by the variegated smoke of propriety?
Thus, although they were repeatedly restrained by Bāṇa and the proud Kumbhāṇḍa,
they nevertheless fled in the ten directions.
Then, on the field of battle, the blessed Lord Rudra— the wielder of the Pināka bow, the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes—
himself arrived to fight along with Guha.
With the vast masses of rays from his limbs, which were as radiant as a heap of snow,
the Lord of the World seemed to adorn the world with abundant prosperity.
It was rippled by his bracelets, armlets, earrings, and circles of serpents,
which appeared like the wavering columns of smoke from the fire that consumed Tripura.

With the circles of light from his neck, he was like the Puṣkarāvartaka clouds— the companions at the onset of the dissolution of the world— which serve as dark blue garments for the maidens of the quarters.
The sprout of the crescent moon shines forth from his tightly bound mass of matted hair,
while the illusion of a turban is created by the surging foam of the celestial river.
On a radiant chariot yoked with elephants named Nandi and lions,
he filled the sky as if he were a personified mass of the fire of his wrath.
Beholding Hara accompanied by Kumāra, who was resplendent with his victory over Tāraka,
Hari remained unshaken and readied his own bow.
In the tumultuous display of battle by the enraged Khaṇḍaparaśu himself,
living beings felt a fear that an untimely dissolution of the world was beginning.
Then Śiva filled Kṛṣṇa with showers of golden arrows,
which resembled the many crests of fire fanned forth from his third eye.
Surrounded by those fierce arrows released from his formidable arms, made manifest by their speed,
they were like serpents encircling him as if snapped by the drawing of his bowstring.
Janārdana released the Parjanya weapon at Rudra— a formidable array of thousands of torrents of arrows, fierce and roaring with a mighty thunder.
Pervaded by that destructive weapon, the enemy of Tripura discharged the fiery weapon (āgneya-astra), which terrified the three worlds.
Surrounded by a circle of flames, the one whose banner is Garuḍa, together with his elder brother,
assumed the splendor of a lion confined within a golden cage.
When that weapon had been neutralized by Murāri with the Vāruṇa weapon,
the Three-eyed Lord fought with the Paiśāca, Raudra, and Āṅgirasa weapons.
Having quickly warded off those weapons with the *saura*, *vāyavya*, and *vāsava* [missiles], he,
overwhelmed by rage, fixed an arrow capable of destroying Tripura.
When the enemy of Andhaka had finally established a bond of friendship with him after a long time,
Hari rendered him, who was expanding his weapons, agitated by his own yawning.
At the repeated, terrible roar of the Śārṅga bow and the Pāñcajanya conch,
and as that fearsome sound expanded, all living beings were seized by a profound dread.
Then Guha, enraged, advanced against Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and Pradyumna on a chariot driven by Kumbhāṇḍa that possessed great speed.
Struck by those weapons— wind, fire, and rain—
he produced a state of confusion and upheaval in the world with his masses of blazing missiles.
The six-faced god also shone, surrounded by those various gold-feathered arrows,
as if out of affection he had returned once more to his own birthplace, that excellent field of arrows.
The destroyer of Tāraka discharged the fierce Brahmāśiras weapon,
by whose blazing flames even the mountains attained the status of Mount Sumeru.
When that fire of the weapon had been unleashed, agitating all things with its initiation for the destruction of the universe, Hari took up his discus.
That terrible weapon, which destroys all other weapons and possesses a discus as fierce as the sun,
was seized by Hari’s staff-like arm, extinguishing its fiery radiance.
When that manifestation of weapons had been cut apart by the flashing edges of the wheel's spokes,
Guha seized his cruel spear, the destroyer of Mount Krauñca.
It is adorned with rows of jewels that shine like the terrifying tusks of Death,
and decorated with red silk scarves that resemble the blood-stained corners of the eyes of the stars.
Kārttikeya hurled that bell, which resounded with a multitude of bells,
as it cried out like a hungry creature eager to swallow the three worlds.
In the mouth of Mahākāla— terrifying with eyebrows and beard like clouds and with a blazing tip of light— he made the sky appear as if it were the tongue lolling out.
"May there be well-being! May there be well-being for the Unfallen One!"—thus was it proclaimed by the gods in heaven.
That spear, directed toward Kṛṣṇa, shone with speed like a flash of lightning.
Struck by the *huṃ* syllable of Kṛṣṇa, she became fruitless from that moment,
like a hope placed in a deceitful-hearted man by a simpleton once it has been gained.
Then the wielder of the discus, fashioning his wrath into a ring,
glanced at Guha with a sidelong look and set his mind upon slaying him.
Naked, with disheveled hair, dark-complexioned and red-eyed,
she stood before him for the protection of the prince like a personified power.
"Go away! Go away!"—thus was she repeatedly rebuked by the serpent Kāliya with words of malice; yet, even though she was being warded off, she did not withdraw from that spot.
In the meantime, Bāṇa himself appeared amidst the armies with deep and resonant roars like the thundering of clouds and shrill cries from the shore.
Seated upon the back of the peacock of Kumāra,
he shone like a mass of dark clouds rising over the slope of Mount Añjana.
Approaching Kṛṣṇa, he who was exalted by the strength of his many arms said: "Alas!
With your destruction now imminent, you are flourishing like a lamp."
"I have slain him in this foreign land, unknown to his friends;
having lost his kinsman, you will surely find it difficult to survive."

it resounded with a deep roar like the thundering of clouds at the time of universal dissolution.

Then, in that great sacrifice of battle— where the clashing of weapons and missiles formed a mass of tangled flames, where the sword served as the sacrificial post, blood was the clarified butter, and the bow was the offering-spoon— the consecrated Bali shone forth.
From here, as Śakra, Arka, and Dahana discharged arrows from the mouths of the Asuras,
a terrible destruction of both armies occurred when a darkness of shafts was produced.
Then the gods, torn by the Daityas' missiles and swords, fled in all directions, terrified and overwhelmed with shame at the mere thought of protecting their own bodies.
When Śakra had his chariot shattered and fled, when Dahana sought refuge in the dense forest, when Māruta desisted from the battle, and when Yama had adopted a state of tranquility; Bhmj_19.1610.
The heroic Bali, lord of the three worlds, ruled over the thirty gods,
having placed his commands upon the heads of all the sovereigns of the entire universe.
When the kingdom of the gods had been reduced to mere legend and the realm of the enemies of the gods was vast,
the gods, seeking protection, went to Nārāyaṇa at the word of the Four-faced One.
O Blessed One, having been entreated by the gods, the omnipresent Lord, whose form was unmanifest,
entered the womb of Aditi through yoga for a period of a thousand years.
Then that Kāśyapa was born as Viṣṇu, dark-complexioned and possessing a dwarf form; he became the foremost in the world, a child most excellent among the dwellers of heaven.
In the meantime, the wise Bali had been initiated for the horse sacrifice;
he was like a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpadruma*) to supplicants, bestowing all their desires.
The god who has Bṛhaspati as his friend went himself to that sacrificial ground and entered it with three peaks, like a crown, a diadem, and a staff for a parasol.
Beholding him— dark-complexioned, with eyes like lotus petals and moving, curling locks of hair— the fish, filled with loveliness, became motionless.
Approaching the lord of the Daityas, that Great-Souled One in the form of a dwarf spoke with sweet and noble words, as if raining down nectar.
The sacrifice of Mahendra, Kubera, Candra, Varuṇa,
and Brahmā took place, and your own ritual shines forth preeminently.
Hearing these words of Vāmana, "Among sacrifices this Aśvamedha is the best, just as you are among embodied beings," Baḍi (or Bali), his soul purified, replied: Bhājana 19.1620.
O virtuous one, this vision of yours delights my mind;
to whom would your speech—not a mere stream of nectar poured through the shell of an ear—be not dear?
"What do you desire that I may give? For to great-souled ones such as you, even the body itself is not something that should not be given, much less external things for long."
When Baḍi had spoken thus, Vāmana replied with affection,
repeatedly making the sky appear as if washed with milk by the luster of his teeth.
"O sweet-spoken one, let three paces of land be granted by you to me for the sake of my teacher;
beyond this, I consider your favor toward me to be great."
Having heard this, Bāli, his mind filled with wonder, spoke with a smile:
"Bāli is a donor."
"You are the seeker; how can the three steps be given?"
"O Sage, accept from me this cherished and great honor as you desire;
even this earth, with its oceans and sovereign mountains, is but a trifle for you who bestow jewels."
Even though he was being urged thus, when Hari did not ask for anything more,
Baḍi (Bali) then offered water for his hands with his face bowed in shame.
Then the omnipresent Lord, who embodies all the gods, increased in size;
in an instant, he pervaded the earth with his feet and the heavens with his head.
As he grew, causing the three worlds to tremble,
his foot became a measuring-staff for the cosmic egg, a pillar reaching into the intermediate space.
"This entire world is not enough for me until my two feet are fully filled"—
as if saying this, he spoke through the sounds of mountains trembling and rolling.
That jewel which was formerly in his crown has now become a pearl;
the circle of light from his smile is upon his face; and even the conch shell has gradually settled upon his chest.
In the sky, that very moon became for him—a supreme doer of harm—the white lotus garland upon his thigh. (Bhājana-vyūha 19.1632)
When his two lotus-feet were washed by Brahmā with water,
the Ganges was born in the world as a garland upon the matted locks of Śiva.
Thus, having traversed the three worlds and seized [the city] from the lord of the Daityas in an instant,
he assigned its location in the subterranean realm named Sutala.
Oh, how vast is the being of the powerful Bali, that great ocean!
By which, through the binding of his own body, the remainder of his vow for giving was purified.
The gods, gandharvas, siddhas, cāraṇas, and kiṃnaras became filled with wonder, overjoyed, ashamed, and likewise trembling.
Having slain the hosts of the sons of Diti, he established the livelihood for the Bāḍavas:
namely, offerings made without faith, gifts given without faith, and likewise funeral rites (śrāddha) performed by those ignorant of the Vedas.
Whatever was without mantras or vows, whatever sacrifice and so forth lacked sacrificial fees,
and whatever else was devoid of ritual procedure— all that Hari bestowed upon him.
Then, having settled the gods in their own respective positions,
he bestowed upon the lord of the gods a splendor as radiant as a garland.
Thus, this meritorious account of the deeds of the Lord, the Consort of Kamalā, has been told in connection with his manifestation; it is the destroyer of all sins.

May the most wondrous form of the Blessed One bring about the pacification of all afflictions for us—his form which, with streams of pure luster from the nails of his feet raised playfully as he strides across the three worlds, creates upon the crown of the cosmic egg the graceful sport of the banner-like celestial river (Gaṅgā) flowing forth; and whose navel-region, resembling a blossoming Brahma-lotus, holds the solar disc as it rests there.
***** The Manifestation of Vāma // 50 // Thus ends the Harivaṃśa in its entirety within the Bhāratamañjarī composed by Kṣemendra.
There was a native of Kaśmīra named Prakāśendra, who was a repository of virtues.
He is a wish-fulfilling tree for the fulfillment of the various intentions of the multitude of those in need.
The brahmins, always satisfied by his complete generosity, said to him:
"You are indeed Indra; however, you possess one particular virtue that is superior."
In whose house there was an unrestrained sacrificial feast of food for the twice-born, possessing noble and abundant riches of virtue like Mount Meru.
During a solar eclipse, having given three hundred thousand [gold pieces] and three black antelope skins,
he stood for a moment with his face bowed in shame, thinking, "I am a giver of very little."
Having installed deities for the victory of Svayambhū and Śambhu,
he gave a fourth part of ten million [gold pieces] to the gods, the twice-born, monasteries, and other institutions.
Having personally worshipped Śarva with a torrent of flowing tears,
he embraced him firmly with both arms and passed away right there.
His son, named Kṣemendra,
attained a status worthy of being mentioned by name in the assemblies of poets through his service to the learned.
Having heard the science of poetics from Abhinavagupta, the crest-jewel of teachers, who clarifies knowledge and is an ocean of awakening; Bhmj_19.*8 //
He who has attained supreme blessedness through the dust of the lotus feet of the venerable teacher Śrīmad-Bhāgavata-Soma, and who is solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
Once, a brahmin approached him and, with a noble mind, requested that he compose a concise summary of the story of the *Bhārata* for the sake of Rāma’s fame.
He said to him, "I shall indeed perform this first deed for me";
then the son of Satyavatī, the treasury of knowledge, being delighted, granted it to him in a dream.
"Having paid homage to that granter of boons, I am ready for what you desire";
having said this, he praised the body of the sage seen in his dream.
Homage to you, Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, who bears matted locks tawny like a mass of flames from the fire of wisdom; though black, you possess a radiance that is not black.
Homage to you, whose radiance is variegated by the light of your luster-filled beard,
and whose splendor has arisen from the pollen of the lotus of the Goddess of Speech (Vāgīśvarī) within your mouth.
Homage to him whose solar radiance has been completely absorbed through meditative absorption at the junction of day and night,
and whose eyes are like lamps that dispel the darkness of the three worlds.
Homage to him who has a thousand branches, who is the tree in the grove of Dharma,
whose flowers are the establishment of sentient beings, and who bears the fruit of nirvāṇa.
Homage to him who wears the black antelope skin, who dwells in the grove of Bodhanandana,
and who is as if pervaded by a swarm of bees seeking his holy fragrance.
Homage to him who is adorned by the rays of his sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), which has the form of a crescent moon;
he who, through contact with it, possesses the stainless radiance of a swan.
Homage to the one who is the full moon for the ocean of scriptures filled with the rivers of knowledge;
to the creator of the poet’s craft, whose essence is the nectar of ambrosia.
Homage to Vyāsa, who dwells in truth, who delights in the play of his own self-manifestation,
who is the abode of austerities, and who removes the exhaustion of saṃsāra.

***** The Hymn of Eight Verses to Vyāsa ***** Having thus composed the "Eight Verses on Vyāsa," he further created the *Mahābhārata-mañjarī*, a river that flows with the nectar of joy for the wise. (Bhājana 19.21)
This *Mahābhārata-mañjarī*, the work of Kṣemendra—also known as Vyāsadāsa, the son of Prakāśendra—is hereby completed.
Oh, how wondrous is this clarity of the Sarasvatī of poets, by which impurity is instantly produced upon the faces of the wicked! (Bhājana 19.1)
Upon the mirror-surface of my words, this Mahābhārata—though it is a world-elephant with all its limbs intact—is seen as if it could be grasped within a single fist. (Bhājana 19.2)
Having enjoyed the earth girdled by the four oceans and enriched with jewels, the Kaurava fell with broken thighs and was devoured by wolves in a place devoid of attendants;

Vijaya, the conqueror of the world, was defeated by cowherds; and the Vṛṣṇis were destroyed by shepherds. Therefore, having reflected deeply upon all this for a long time, let the mind be directed toward peace. 19.3.
May the splendors of Śauri’s body— stealing the beauty of the blooming blue lotus,

resembling swarms of bees greedy for the pollen of his own navel-lotus, and repeatedly creating the illusion of musk-leaf patterns upon Lakṣmī’s moon-like face which is as pure as the lunar orb— protect you. May this person, sprinkled by the meritorious waters of the holy sites (tīrthas) of Viṣṇu’s stories, [attain] the grace of Lakṣmī.
Even though he is but a common talker, Kṣemendra has today attained the status of a lord among poets.
May there be auspiciousness!
